toc.title: 3. Journaling your trauma before you have the capacity for it
What these five have in common

sections.title: What does "working within your capacity" mean?
Should I journal about my trauma?
Is a morning routine a bad idea?

blocks.p: The self-help industry sells doing as the cure: more habits, more discipline, more effort.

And that makes sense, right? Nothing changes unless you do something different. So it really comes down to two things: what that different thing is, and whether it actually leads to the change you want.
But here's the catch. If your nervous system is already overwhelmed, already running hot in sympathetic fight-or-flight or dropped into a dorsal shutdown, more doing isn't automatically the answer.
Doing more can lead to more overwhelm, more frustration, and more defeat.

I want to walk through five common self-help habits you might already be doing that could be unintentionally making things worse. By the way, this isn't therapy, and it isn't an attack on these practices across the board. Some of them are great for people who already have the capacity for them. I'm more concerned about you if you're stuck in a defensive state, because that's when the thing that's supposed to help can actually keep you stuck.

This one looks like standing in front of a mirror, repeating "I am worthy, I am safe, I am enough" while your body is screaming the opposite. Or trying to swap out every negative thought for a positive one. Or using gratitude journaling as an emotional override.
"What's the problem with positive thinking, Justin?"

Well, the first thing that comes to mind is that it's not real. Thinking something positive, even over and over, doesn't make it so. And no, you can't summon positivity from the universe through your thinking. That's called wishing. Is it okay to wish for things? Yeah, sure, go right ahead, especially on your birthday. Journal about your gratitude when you actually have gratitude to journal about. Tell yourself something nice in the mirror when you have something nice to say. When it's real, do those things.

But when your body is in a defensive state, you probably lack the positivity and the nice things to say to yourself. So when you tell yourself the opposite of what you feel, you create a mismatch between your thoughts and your nervous system state. Your brain says I'm fine, everything's going to be okay. Your body doesn't believe it. In essence, you're lying to yourself. You can't trick your body into safety by changing the words in your head.

And that mismatch isn't neutral. I'd say it's disrespectful. You're basically telling your body to shut up. That's not safety, that's invalidation. And invalidation just adds friction and makes things worse. I'd bet you've already gotten plenty of that invalidation from someone else in your life. So the sooner you stop doing it to yourself, the better.

Instead of forcing positivity, try honest acknowledgment. "My body feels tense right now. That makes sense given what I've been through." That's not negativity, that's accuracy. And accuracy is what builds trust between you and your nervous system. I hear it from clients and [Unstucking Academy](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator) students all the time. Just acknowledging and normalizing what they're feeling brings the intensity down.

blocks.prompt: Try it now. What is your body feeling right now, said plainly, with no fixing? ("My body feels tense right now.")

blocks.p: If you're not sure which state you're in, [reading your own nervous system](hub:read) is the place to start.

I need to tread carefully here, because people absolutely love their breathing methods. Wim Hof. Intense pranayama. Holotropic breathwork. Box breathing with long holds. They all come with big promises.

So what's the problem? Controlled breathing runs into the same trouble as forced positive thinking. It rejects your body's natural state. Your thinking mind tells your body, I know better than you, you're breathing wrong.

Sit with that for a second. Do you, in your conscious thinking mind, actually know how much oxygen you need right now? Or do the unconscious, automatic systems that have been doing it your whole life know better? To me, the answer is pretty obvious.

Your body is in a dominant defensive state, and it breathes in response to what that state needs right now. Logically, yeah, we assume that if we change the breath, we change the state. And, kind of. But the dominant state comes right back, doesn't it? In this exact moment, extending your exhale might help you settle into a little more stillness. Right now, deeper breaths into your chest might boost your mobilization. But your body may not need those. And again, you're adding friction to the self-regulation process.

So I guide clients and Unstucking Academy students to just notice their natural breath. And you know what happens? It changes on its own, in a fairly predictable way. People running high in sympathetic fight-or-flight, breathing tight and high in the chest, will notice the breath drifting down into the belly. People in shutdown, breathing shallow, will notice more room opening up in the chest. But they don't plan it. It happens by itself, once we pay attention and stay in the present moment. That's the heart of [somatic self-regulation](piece:somatic-self-regulation).

blocks.h: 3. Journaling your trauma before you have the capacity for it

blocks.p: This is where people sit down and write out detailed accounts of their worst experiences. "Get it all out on paper," they say. Or they use prompts like "what's your earliest painful memory," or "write a letter to your abuser."
It looks like deep work. And maybe some people are ready for it. But there's a good chance they're not. And because it looks like the real work, you might push yourself into it before you're ready.
This is memory excavation without a regulated baseline. You're jumping in the pool without knowing how to swim, or where the ladder is to climb back out.

Writing traumatic details in detail lights up a lot of the same networks as living them. Your body doesn't really tell the difference between remembering and reliving. So if you don't have the ventral vagal capacity to stay anchored in the present, you're not processing anything. You might be re-traumatizing yourself.

It's the same problem you run into with approaches like EMDR or trauma-focused CBT when they're used without enough regulation first. The method isn't bad. It's the sequence. We need present-moment grounding first, and ideally more capacity, before we go into the painful stuff. It's why [revisiting trauma too fast can backfire](piece:therapy-retraumatization).
A couple of easy alternatives if you want to journal, or tweak how you already do it.
Journal on the present moment. What do you hear? What do you see? How's your body breathing? What thoughts are passing through? Is there an emotion in you right now?
Or write about something hard, but keep it contained. Less detail, fewer words. As you write about the past, stay anchored to the present.

Write a little. When you feel activation rising, pause or stop. Recover. Then continue when you're ready, and pause again when you need to. Pausing and recovering after a few words is way more useful than forcing your way through five pages of past agony and just feeling all of it again right now.
There's nothing wrong with routine and structure. That might be exactly what you need. I've got my own little routines I like to follow.

But ask yourself what the routine is actually for. Are you suppressing emotion through a controlled routine? That's okay for coping, but it's not the same as actually making change, which is kind of the whole point of self-help, right?

Do you really need the 6 am smoothie, or is it just something to focus on instead of the stress and overwhelm that actually needs your attention? Do you really need to keep a gratitude journal at 6:15, or is it okay to look out the window in silence and admit that life kind of sucks right now? Are you taking the cold shower for the health benefits, or to shock your emotions out of your system for a while? Are you doing all of it because it feels right, or because someone popular online does the same thing?

For a regulated nervous system, or one with mild dysregulation, these routines can be grounding. Totally fine. But for a dysregulated one, they're at best a coping skill, and at worst, one more demand on a system that can't take any more. One more thing to get excited about and then fail at (or feel like you're failing at).

And then what happens when you miss a day, or blend the wrong stuff into the smoothie? A shame spiral kicks in. Now, the thing that was supposed to help you is generating the exact sympathetic arousal and dorsal collapse it was supposed to prevent. Those feelings, the shame and the regret and the pressure, they aren't new. They were already in there, masked by the routine. When you miss it, they surface.

So, again, nothing wrong with a routine. I think they're a good idea. Yes, leave the house on time to get to work and get the kids to school. Yes, wake up early enough to get ready. Yes, eat breakfast. Basic stuff, and a routine helps.

But inside that routine, check in with your body and what it actually needs. You might want to start the day super productive, but if you're sluggish, that's not going to happen. Maybe you need quiet, dim lighting to wake up. (That sluggish, offline morning is often a [dorsal shutdown](piece:dorsal-vagal-shutdown) morning.) You might want slow and calm, but if you wake up with stress, that's not happening either, and maybe you need to move first.

You gotta listen to your body. You don't decide it. Your body's state does. And it changes with your capacity, the seasons, and even daylight savings. So instead of fixed and rigid, leave a little room for spontaneity inside the basics.
Yes, I want you to feel your feelings too. But only when you're connected enough to the present moment and actually ready. If not, you risk opening the floodgates and drowning.

"Feel your feelings" assumes you have the distress tolerance to stay present while you feel the emotion. It assumes your safety state capacity can handle it. And maybe it just can't yet. So you end up right back where you started.

The alternative is very simple emotional balancing. Touch the edge of the feeling, then come back to safety in the present. Back and forth. Like dipping your toe in the water instead of diving into the deep end.

Instead of feeling the feeling as a raw sensation in the body, maybe just start by acknowledging it as a fact, without denying it. Instead of diving into the deep end of [depression](piece:depression-polyvagal-theory) and staying submerged in the heaviness and emptiness and numbness, just acknowledge it truthfully. "I feel depressed."

Then shift your focus back to the present, like the sounds around you and the view out your window. Once you can acknowledge it, you can start going a little deeper into the emotional waters. How it shows up in your body generally, then more specifically, and then the actual sensations, all while balancing back to safety.
The ability to feel your feelings, to sit with it, gets built up gradually through short, consistent practice. Not one big cathartic explosion.

A small, practical way to be with a difficult emotion without going under. Use this when the emotion is at a tolerable level or when you intentionally choose to feel into it, like during a self-regulation practice.

ol: Name it, plainly. "I feel anxious." "I feel heavy." No fixing, no story.
Let your attention touch just the edge of it, for a breath or two.
Come back to something present and neutral. A sound. Your feet on the floor. The light in the room.
Go again only if you want to. Toe in the water, not a dive.

blocks.p: Cost: about two minutes · When: whenever a feeling rises · State: any defensive state emotion you can tolerate easily, then back toward balanced

blocks.why: Touching a feeling, then coming back to safety, is what your practice does too, at the pace your check-ins point to.

blocks.h: What these five have in common

blocks.p: What do these five share? Every one of them asks you to go beyond what you may be capable of right now.

Here's my recommendation. Whatever you're doing to work on yourself, whether it's these five, or therapy, or a coach, or talking to your pastor, or joining the Unstucking Academy, work within your capacity. Don't push too far or too fast.

And remember, the self-help gurus are teaching you from their own capacity. They can think positively. Good for them. They love controlling their breath and get something out of it. They can journal about their pain. They stick to their strict morning routine. They feel their feelings through long meditations. Outstanding. I'm happy for them.
I honestly don't care whether you do these things or not. It's up to you. I care that you're working within your capacity.

The other thing they share is that they put your thinking brain, as the expert, in charge of what your body actually needs. Your thinking brain decides it knows best about your breath, or your morning, or your feelings. When really, your body might be saying, "You know, actually, we need something else."
None of this will settle a sensitized nervous system instantly, and it won't replace therapy if that's what your situation calls for.

So if you recognize yourself in one of these five habits, that's not a reason to feel shame. Especially if you like doing them. And if you can now see that one of them isn't really helping, that's not a reason for shame either. That's just awareness. And awareness is the first step toward doing something different, right?
New to all of this? Start with the [polyvagal theory introduction](piece:snb101-polyvagal-101-foundations).

Yes, it can keep you stuck. Forcing positivity, controlled breathwork, journaling trauma before you have the capacity for it, rigid routines, and "just feel your feelings" all push an already-defensive nervous system to do more than it can hold, or they override what your body is doing for a reason. A nervous system stuck in defense settles through safety and honest acknowledgment, not more force.

blocks.h3: What does "working within your capacity" mean?

blocks.p: It means matching the practice to what your nervous system can actually handle right now, and stopping before you tip into overwhelm. You touch the edge of a hard feeling or memory, then come back to the present, building tolerance in small, repeatable doses rather than in one flood.

Only when they're true. Saying something kind you actually feel is fine. Forcing the opposite of your real state is where it backfires, because the mismatch reads as invalidation to the body and adds friction. Honest acknowledgment builds more trust than a positive line you don't believe.

Not by itself. For a regulated nervous system, it can help. But in a strong defensive state, forcing a breathing pattern overrides what your body is doing for a reason, and the dominant state usually comes right back. Noticing your natural breath and letting it change on its own tends to be gentler and last longer.

blocks.h3: Should I journal about my trauma?

blocks.p: Only with enough present-moment capacity to stay anchored while you do it. Writing traumatic details can activate many of the same networks as reliving them. Keep it contained, pause when activation rises, recover, and build capacity before you go into detail.

blocks.h3: Is a morning routine a bad idea?

blocks.p: No, basic structure helps. The question is your motivation. A routine used to suppress emotion or perform can become one more demand and one more thing to fail at. Keep the structure, but check what your body actually needs that morning instead of forcing a fixed script.
